blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the **kth largest** element — the one that would sit at position k if the array were sorted from largest to smallest. Duplicates count: in `[3, 3, 1]` the 2nd largest is 3. Can you do it **without fully sorting**?

blocks.alt: The array [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4] with k = 2. Sorted from largest to smallest it is [6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1], so the 2nd largest is 5.

elements.text: Kth Largest Element in an Array
elements.originalText: Kth Largest Element in an Array

blocks.code:
Input:  nums = [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2
Output: 5

Input:  nums = [3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], k = 4
Output: 4      largest first: 6, 5, 5, 4, ...

blocks.text: Sort the array; the kth largest is `k` places from the end.

blocks.code:
def find_kth_largest(nums, k):
    return sorted(nums)[len(nums) - k]   # kth from the end

blocks.text: **Time O(n log n), space up to O(n)** depending on the sort. It does far more than asked: it puts **every** element in order when we only care about one position.
2. Optimal: keep only the k largest in a min-heap

Walk the array while holding the **k largest values seen so far** in a **min-heap** (a structure that always hands you its smallest value in O(1), and adds or removes in O(log size)). When the heap grows past `k`, throw out its smallest value — it can't be among the top k. At the end, the heap holds exactly the k largest values, and its **smallest** one is the answer.

blocks.alt: Processing [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4] with k = 2. The min-heap of size 2 ends holding 5 and 6. Its smallest value, 5, is the 2nd largest.
blocks.caption: The heap never holds more than k values, so each step costs O(log k).

blocks.text: JavaScript has no built-in heap, so the JavaScript version includes a small one; the other languages use their standard priority queues.
**Time O(n log k), space O(k).** When k is small this is close to linear. But every element still pays a log k heap operation — can we get to plain O(n)?

Borrow quicksort's partition step — but only follow **one side**. Pick a **pivot** value and rearrange the current range into three zones: values **bigger** than the pivot, values **equal** to it, and values **smaller** (exactly the Dutch flag from *Sort 0s, 1s and 2s*).

blocks.alt: A range split into three zones: bigger than the pivot, equal to the pivot, and smaller than the pivot. The target index k − 1 falls in one zone, and only that zone is kept.
blocks.caption: In largest-first order the kth largest sits at index k − 1. After one partition we know which zone that index is in.

elements.text: k − 1 in the left zone   →  search only the left zone
elements.originalText: k − 1 in the left zone   →  search only the left zone

elements.text: k − 1 in the middle zone →  the answer is the pivot
elements.originalText: k − 1 in the middle zone →  the answer is the pivot

elements.text: k − 1 in the right zone  →  search only the right zone
elements.originalText: k − 1 in the right zone  →  search only the right zone

blocks.text: Each round throws away everything outside one zone. With a **random** pivot, a round shrinks the range by about half on average, so the total work is about n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ **2n**. The three-way split also keeps rounds fast when there are many equal values.

blocks.caption: The simulator picks the middle element as the pivot so every run is repeatable; the code below picks a random one. Watch the three zones grow from both ends, and the search range shrink after each round.

blocks.text: **Time O(n) on average, space O(1).** The worst case is O(n²) — if every pivot were the worst possible value — but with a random pivot that is astronomically unlikely. It rearranges `nums`; copy the array first if the caller needs it unchanged.

rows.timeWhy: Sorting orders **all n** elements, though only one position matters.
rows.spaceWhy: Up to O(n), depending on the language's sort.

rows.approach: Optimal: a min-heap of the k largest
rows.timeWhy: Each of the **n** elements costs one heap push or pop of **log k**.
rows.spaceWhy: The heap never holds more than **k** values.

rows.timeWhy: Each partition keeps only one side: n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ **2n**. A run of bad pivots could reach O(n²), which a random pivot makes very unlikely.
rows.spaceWhy: Partitioning swaps **in place** in the input.

blocks.text: In an interview, mention both: the heap is simple, predictable and great when `k` is small or the data arrives as a stream; quickselect is the fastest on average when the whole array is in memory.

items: **All equal** — `[7, 7, 7, 7]` returns 7 for any k; the equal zone ends the search in one round.
